1 I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. 2 And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God. - Romans 12:1-2 (KJV)

 Christians always want to know what the will of God is for their lives and this verse tells you. God wants you – not what you can do for Him, but He wants you in a personal relationship with Him, by giving yourself wholly to Him. If you will give yourself to God, and do what the Holy Spirit tells you to do, God will be pleased with you, and will lead you through life, and your life will be better than you ever dreamed (Jeremiah 29:11). People think that giving their lives over to the Lord will cause them to live in a hut in Africa, or something, but that is not true (James 1:17). God will first of all put His desires in your heart, then He will give you the desires of your heart, and you will love it. Serving God and following Him is not something to be dreaded, but is something to desire, as it is wonderful.

 When you give yourself to God as a living sacrifice, then what He wants you to do is renew your mind by studying the bible, as the bible will tell you what God wants you to do. As you study the bible, the Holy Spirit will make it come alive to you, and you will come to know God in an intimate way, and build a relationship with Him. Studying God’s Word, and praying to Him, will bring you close to God, and that is what He wants, and what Jesus came and died for (John 3:16), to bring you into fellowship with the Father and Jesus (John 17:3). God loves His children so much that he died to have this fellowship with you, and if He gets your love, He will also get your service. Praise God for Jesus.

Rather than dual booting, you could try mounting a physical drive in VirtualBox and installing Linux there. That way you can seamlessly integrate your current windows desktop environment with the linux of your ultimate choosing. Eventually one day, when you decide to ditch windows, you have the option to boot directly to the Linux drive.

I've successfully done the old switcharoo when my laptop needed a reinstall but had no CD drive, I put the drive in my desktop PC, mounted it as a raw disk in virtualbox, installed the OS, and then physically disconnected the drive and put it in the laptop. Booted like a charm.

Gonna warn ya that the vast majority of distributions are pushing systemd HARD, and if they aren't, they're probably going to. I'm not too convinced that this is a good thing, but it is what it is. Your choice of distributions is going to be severely limited if this is a deal-breaker. Those that have a more traditional init.d will probably be those that tend more towards a traditional Unix experience, e.g. Slackware, or may somehow be niche in a way that is not suited towards systemd (some super-compact distros come to mind, though I don't know what the difference is in terms of disk/RAM footprint between systemd and init.d). Either way, I don't think you're going to find a perfect candidate, and may have to trade - possibly a lot - for init.d in particular. In particular I'm pretty sure that most "easy to use," bright and friendly, hardware auto-detect-y installations that are popular are going to be moving in systemd's direction. There is some hope of an after-installation swap from init.d to systemd, though, at least if someone is willing to maintain such a beast for the distro you choose, but I have no idea how good of an idea it is - that strikes me as risky.

I would strongly suggest that you consider what someone else suggested - try them out on VirtualBox. This is a good idea overall these days, since VirtualBox is a really good option and has been for the last few years. However, I'd put a twist on it. Once you have a better idea of what you think you will like, see if you can find something with a more traditional init.d system. Although you may not be successful, you won't have to install and wipe 20 different distros in the attempt.

Though one last word of advice - if you do choose a distro that isn't one of the really big ones (e.g. Fedora, Debian, Ubuntu, etc.) see if you can get a feel for the community and likely longevity of it. I don't think you want to invest months of effort into finding the perfect distribution only to see it implode because one of the two maintainers was snagged off the deck of a ship by a shark and dragged to the depths to be dinner.

Yes, I'm perfectly sane, whyever do you ask?

If I were you, I'd start by installing a virtual machine handler, create a linux distro, and then run all of your work through that. The only thing you use the host OS for, is to boot the VM. Then you can test out different flavors (or a windows 8.1 distro) and see what you like. By the time the decision comes around, you'll be able to configure your box with the distro you most feel comfortable with.
You should use Slackware! It's stable, secure, easy to upgrade, and won't be having systemd any time soon. It's about the most Unixy distro of Linux there is.

Remember if you start with an easy to use distro like Mint or Debian you can install Virtualbox and test out the other distros like Slackware/Arch/Gentoo or BSD.

Good Luck!
